item.title: 3.1 Policy
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 1: Program Foundation. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

In an organization without an AI SBOM policy, developers deploy AI systems without being aware of the license obligations of models and datasets. In AI, what must be tracked goes beyond code. Model weights, training datasets, and the Model Tree of models derived from other models each have their own licenses, and non-standard licenses that restrict the purpose of use, such as the Llama Community License or the RAIL family, are common. Missing these obligations leads to copyright disputes, violations of use restrictions, and termination of business contracts.

item.title: 3.10 Governance
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 4: Governance. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

Governance is the framework that brings all the preceding clauses together and ensures responsible development, deployment, and management across the AI system lifecycle. If the policy (3.1) sets the principles and license obligations (3.5) and the AI SBOM (3.9) create individual processes, governance manages them so that they work consistently even as regulations change and models are replaced.

item.title: 3.5 License Obligations
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 2: AI Extension Processes. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

License obligations are where the AI SBOM guide extends ISO/IEC 5230 the most. Whereas traditional open source compliance reviewed the licenses of code, in AI the review targets grow to four: the AI system’s code, model weights, datasets (including training, testing, and verification datasets), and the license of the AI system itself. Because it is common for one model to be derived from several other models, each upstream model in the Model Tree has its own license.

item.title: 3.7 Access
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 3: Operating Structure. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

Organizations that exchange AI systems in the supply chain need to confirm each other’s compliance. For that, a channel for external inquiries must be publicly available, and the organization must be ready to respond to those inquiries. Access ensures both directions.

3.7 requires two things: publicly identifying a means by which a third party can make an AI SBOM compliance inquiry, and maintaining an internal process to respond effectively to those inquiries. For AI, inquiries also cover AI-specific information such as model and dataset licenses, training data provenance, and model cards.

item.title: OWASP AIBOM Generator
item.description:
Overview

OWASP AIBOM Generator is an open source tool that takes a Hugging Face model ID, retrieves the model card metadata, and generates an AI SBOM in CycloneDX format. It is maintained by the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, and its distinguishing feature is scoring how complete the generated BOM is.

Unlike cdxgen, which identifies dependencies quickly but leaves licenses empty, this tool fills in the license, authors, and external references written in the model card. It is a good starting point for the license review required by 3.5 License Obligations.

item.title: Program Foundation
item.description: This is Phase 1 of the implementation roadmap. It defines the scope of the program (3.4), establishes the policy (3.1), and secures the competence and awareness of participants (3.2, 3.3). All subsequent clauses operate on this foundation.

item.title: 3.2 Competence
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 1: Program Foundation. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

If the policy (3.1) sets out what must be done, competence ensures there are people who can do it. AI SBOM compliance requires broader knowledge than open source compliance, which dealt only with code licenses. Practitioners must judge the licenses of model weights and datasets, interpret model cards, and understand emerging AI regulations and the use restrictions of non-standard licenses.

item.title: 3.6 Transparency Obligations
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 2: AI Extension Processes. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

If license obligations (3.5) ask “do we have the right to use this material,” transparency obligations ask “what must we disclose about this material.” The two obligations come from different sources. License obligations are imposed by copyright holders through contract, and transparency obligations are imposed by regulations through law.

3.6 requires a procedure for reviewing whether there are transparency obligations imposed by regulations. The review covers training, testing, and verification datasets and takes into account the intended use of the model. If the use case for the training data creates a transparency issue (e.g., disclosure obligations to downstream recipients), appropriate risk mitigation measures must be taken. As the EU AI Act begins to fully apply its transparency obligations from August 2026, this clause is becoming more important in practice.

item.title: 3.8 Effectively Resourced
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 3: Operating Structure. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

If competence (3.2) defines “who must be able to do what,” effective resourcing attaches actual people, time, and budget to those roles so that the program works. If policies and procedures exist only on paper with no resources, compliance exists in name only.

3.8 requires assigning accountability for program tasks and allocating sufficient resources. There are five verification materials, covering identification of role owners, provision of staff and funding, access to legal expertise, a procedure for assigning internal responsibilities, and a procedure for remediating non-compliance. The specification cites the resource-related sections (B.4.2, B.4.6) and the human oversight section (B.9.3) of Annex B of ISO/IEC 42001 as references.

item.title: AI Extension Processes
item.description: This is Phase 2 of the implementation roadmap. It is the area where the AI SBOM guide extends ISO/IEC 5230 the most, and it covers license obligations (3.5), transparency obligations (3.6), and AI SBOM creation and management (3.9).

item.title: AI SBOM
item.description:
1. What is an AI SBOM?

An AI SBOM (AI System Bill of Materials) documents a list of every element that makes up an AI system, along with its source and license. It extends the concept of the software SBOM (ISO/IEC 5230 §3.3.1) to AI systems and is the key deliverable for the ISO/IEC 42001 §7.5 (Documented information) requirement.

Why an AI SBOM Is Needed: Transparency and Regulatory Compliance

The AI SBOM is a key means of securing transparency and explainability of AI systems. ISO/IEC 42001 Appendix C.2.11 states transparency and explainability as key objectives of the AI management system.

item.title: cdxgen
item.description:
Overview

cdxgen is the official SBOM generator of the OWASP CycloneDX project. It supports more than 20 languages and package managers, and recent versions provide a dedicated AI BOM mode. It automatically identifies the dependencies of AI applications (PyTorch, Transformers, etc.) and integrates well with CI/CD pipelines.

From an AI SBOM perspective, cdxgen’s strengths are speed and automation. Its weakness is that it does not fill in license information in a default run. The run results below show this characteristic. Whereas OWASP AIBOM Generator centers on model card metadata, cdxgen centers on code and dependencies. Using both together covers both models and dependencies.

item.title: 3. Support
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §7 covers the competence, awareness, communication, and documentation needed to operate the AI management system. From the perspective of open source practitioners, §7.2 (Competence) and §7.5 (Documented information) are the key points of intersection.

2. §7.2 Competence: AI Open Source Management Competence ★

ISO/IEC 42001 requires that persons performing AI-related roles have the necessary competence. From an open source compliance perspective, AI development and operations staff should have the following competencies.

item.title: 3.3 Awareness
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 1: Program Foundation. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

If competence (3.2) deals with “can they do it,” awareness deals with “do they know why they must do it.” It is not enough for participants to know only that the policy exists. Compliance actually works only when they also know how their work contributes to the program and what happens if they do not follow it.

item.title: 3.9 AI SBOM
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 2: AI Extension Processes. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

An AI SBOM (AI System Bill of Materials) is a list of the components that make up an AI system and information about them. Whereas a traditional SBOM records software components, an AI SBOM adds models, weights, datasets, and hyperparameters. 3.9 requires a procedure for creating and managing an AI SBOM.

item.title: Model and Container Scanners (Lab700x, Trivy, Syft)
item.description:
This page introduces analysis and identification tools that complement AI SBOM generation. If the generation tools (OWASP AIBOM Generator, cdxgen) record “what is inside,” these tools look at “whether it is safe” and “which version it is.” The commands and features below are based on each tool’s official documentation (the tools actually run in this guide are OWASP AIBOM Generator and cdxgen).

Lab700x AI SBOM Scanner: Static Analysis of Model Binaries

This tool statically analyzes AI model files themselves to extract information. It examines model binaries such as .safetensors, .pt (PyTorch), and .pkl (Pickle) directly without running them (deep introspection).

item.title: Operations
item.description: This is Phase 3 of the implementation roadmap. You set up a channel for responding to external AI SBOM compliance inquiries (3.7) and assign responsibility, staff, and funding to the program (3.8).

item.title: 3.4 Program Scope
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 1: Program Foundation. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

The program scope determines how far compliance applies. If the scope is vague, it becomes unclear for which AI systems an SBOM must be created and which models’ licenses must be reviewed. Only when the scope is declared first do all subsequent clauses know what they apply to.

3.4 requires declaring the scope that applies to each program. Scope can differ from one organization to another. Some organizations cover a single product line, while others cover an entire department or the entire organization. In AI, the scope decision covers not only internally developed models but also models and datasets brought in from outside and the external release of internal models.

item.title: Governance
item.description: This is Phase 4 of the implementation roadmap. You bring the preceding clauses together into a governance framework across the AI system lifecycle, and review it periodically to reflect emerging AI regulations (3.10).

item.title: AI SBOM Compliance Guide
item.description:
This guide explains, one by one, each requirement of AI System Bill of Materials: Compliance Management Guide for the Supply Chain (Version 1.0), published by the OpenChain AI Work Group. It describes what verification materials each clause requires, how to comply, and what samples and tools can be used directly.

This specification carries the structure of the open source license compliance standard ISO/IEC 5230 (requirements, verification materials, rationale) over to the AI supply chain. It brings into the scope of compliance not only code but also the license and transparency obligations of model weights, training datasets, and the Model Tree.

item.title: Tools
item.description:
This section covers open source tools that automate AI SBOM compliance. For each tool, it summarizes the main features, installation, and usage, along with actual run results. It makes the categories in the automation maturity map of 3.9 AI SBOM concrete, tool by tool.

There is a limit worth stating plainly. Tools generate BOMs automatically, but they cannot guarantee that the licenses in the generated BOM are correct or that no components are missing. In the tool comparison below, OWASP AIBOM Generator fills in the license from the model card, while cdxgen identifies dependencies quickly but leaves the license field empty. Consider this difference when choosing a tool.

item.title: 7. AI Compliance
item.description:
Requirements Covered in This Section

ISO/IEC 42001: §5.2 (AI Policy) · §6.1.2 (AI Risk Assessment) · §7.5 (Documentation) · §8.5 (AI Lifecycle) · §8.6 (AI Data) · §8.8 (External AI Procurement)

AI systems make extensive use of open source frameworks, pre-trained models, and open datasets. Companies that operate an open source management system (ISO/IEC 5230 · 18974) must apply open source compliance principles during the AI system development phase as well. In addition, development environments that leverage AI coding tools (GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) require a new management framework to address license contamination and the introduction of vulnerable packages.
